summary:
West Nusa Tenggara stands under Indonesia's national framework, and no sub-national deviation for this province is recorded: no enacted bylaw, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people in West Nusa Tenggara, and no protective legislation for the province. The province is assessed at the national risk level.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Parliament passed a new Penal Code in December 2022 that took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises consensual sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties reported at up to two years' imprisonment and at up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside the national morality provisions. Aceh punishes homosexuality under sharia law by flogging or imprisonment, and its penalties apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. No equivalent provincial provision for West Nusa Tenggara appears in the sources.

Physical risk is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and August 2026 coverage reports growing repression of Indonesia's transgender community under the framework that governs West Nusa Tenggara. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa and arrested 75 people, and Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called the operation a violation of human rights and privacy. Further raids took place in South Jakarta in February and May 2025.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother in Lima alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes writing or audio-visual material showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents allow only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval.
tangentialFactors:
Social hostility is measured at national scale: Pew data cited for 2025 records 93% of Indonesians labelling homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. Conversion therapy is widely practiced. A visitor's exposure to hostility in West Nusa Tenggara is shaped by these attitudes rather than by any provincial law.

West Nusa Tenggara comprises the two large islands of Lombok and Sumbawa, with an official mid-2025 population estimate of 5,731,110. Ministry of Religious Affairs data for 2022 records 96.88% of residents as Muslim, and the province's character is described as conservative and religious, with the majority Sasak people of Lombok maintaining Wetu Telu, a form of Islam influenced by local beliefs. The provincial economy is dependent on tourism, which concentrates visitors in venues where national enforcement activity is also concentrated.

The comparison with Aceh and South Sumatra sets the outer bound of sub-national risk in Indonesia: those two provinces impose penalties that West Nusa Tenggara does not, and Aceh's religious-law punishments reach foreign visitors present in that province. Raids in Jakarta and the Puncak area show that enforcement against LGBT gatherings is carried out nationally rather than confined to the provinces with their own criminal provisions.

No national law protects residents from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so remedies for workplace, housing or service discrimination are absent at statute level.

Conversion therapy is widely practiced, and August 2026 reporting describes growing repression of the transgender community under official condemnation and the presidential decree of October 2025 that places LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy as a non-military threat.

Residents face exposure under the 2006 pornography statute for written or audio-visual material suggesting same-sex relations, under the March 2016 broadcast ban, and through government blocking of websites and apps carrying LGBTQ-related words. A bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no West Nusa Tenggara bylaw, raid, arrest, prosecution or incident involving transgender people, and no source confirms whether any provincial religious bylaw operates in this province. The absence is recorded from the sources reviewed and is not a finding that none exists.

The sources report the new Penal Code's outside-marriage offence at up to two years' imprisonment and, for complaints lodged by immediate family, at up to one year. Whether these figures are cumulative or alternative is not stated, and enforcement data for West Nusa Tenggara is not available.

Not sourced: whether the presidential decree of October 2025 has been applied in West Nusa Tenggara, the scale and settings of conversion therapy in the province, and whether Indonesian entry screening or visa applications ask travellers about gender identity or transition status.

The Pew figure is a measure of public opinion recorded for 2025, not a measure of legal risk or of reported violence, and no source in the inventory links it to incidents in this province.
